questions.explanation: The single record establishes what can happen, not how often it fails, and the claim on the table is about reliability, which is a rate. A count of comparable households kept over the same years answers it; the family's own fifty years cannot, however long they are, because a run with no failures carries no information about the runs that ended. The tempting reading keeps the fifty years and calls them representative, which mistakes a record that exists for a distribution that was observed.
questions.hint: Ask what the claim needs to know that fifty successful years cannot tell it.
questions.learningObjective: identify the source that would let a general claim rest on a single record

options.misconception: repeats the same single case at a larger scale
options.text: Three neighbours of the same age, all of whom kept bees for decades

options.misconception: asks a rate question and answers it with an opinion
options.text: An expert's view that home beekeeping is generally a safe practice
How often comparable households stopped, counted over the same years

questions.explanation: Credibility is spent, not banked, and this column spends it on a settledness its subject has not earned: a live dispute cannot be closed by the tone of a sentence. The reader who finds a settled question where an open one exists learns to discount the writer generally, including the parts that hold up. The tempting reading hears confidence as the mark of a writer who has read everything, but confidence is what the absence of a hedge sounds like, and sparing a reader the work of weighing evidence is not a courtesy when the weighing is the only thing standing between them and a mistake.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer's standing with the reader is made of, and where it goes.
questions.learningObjective: identify what unwarranted certainty costs a writer's credibility

options.text: Spent the writer's credibility on a settledness the subject does not allow

options.misconception: takes a bare assertion of certainty as evidence of diligence
options.text: Shown a writer who has read everything, so the reader can rely on the rest

options.misconception: assumes the field has in fact settled the question being disputed
options.text: Matched the confidence of a field that has itself genuinely settled it

options.misconception: counts the saving of effort as though it were a service to the reader
options.text: Spared a busy reader the work of weighing evidence they cannot check

questions.explanation: The calculation carries the criticism and the writer never says the word waste, so the reader performs the verdict and owns it: a conclusion you reach yourself resists argument in a way one handed to you does not. That is what the comparison is doing. The tempting reading hears ridicule aimed at the members, which would make the piece a matter of manners rather than of administration; the target is the allocation of four hours, and the joke is a way of costing it in the reader's own head rather than asserting it.

answer.exemplar: The concession makes the criticism that follows checkable instead of hostile, and it proves the reviewer applied the standard to the piece's own weakest point rather than only to the writer's. A reader who has watched a reviewer concede something real will believe the rest of the note, because a reviewer willing to lose a point on their own side is not the kind of reviewer who invents points on yours.

questions.explanation: A concession is a demonstration that the standard being applied is real, because it is applied in the one place where it costs the reviewer something. Once the piece's own weakness has been named, the remaining criticism arrives as a finding rather than a preference, and a reader has grounds to think the reviewer weighed the piece rather than scored it. The tempting reading calls the concession politeness, or a softener before the attack; it does the opposite work, since a review that never concedes reads as an assessment in which no amount of good work would have passed.
questions.hint: Ask what the concession proves about the standard behind the rest of the note.
questions.learningObjective: explain what a concession does for the credibility of the criticism around it

questions.explanation: Professional distance is a rule about what may colour a description: the writer reports what each side claims without letting a preference decide which claims sound reasonable. It is a limit on description, not a temperature. The tempting reading hears distance as coolness, or as a deferral of judgement to the last paragraph, and a piece that is genuinely neutral would not be one that announces its own neutrality at the end, since announcing it is a verdict after all.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer is forbidden to let alter the description itself.

Reporting each side's claims without letting a preference colour them

options.misconception: assumes neutrality is announced rather than practised
options.text: Staying impersonal until a final paragraph states the writer's own view

questions.explanation: Each of the three hands the reader a limit on the report's own findings: the sample was small, so the figures are indicative; a specified group will be unconvinced, so the disagreement is located; an earlier estimate was wrong, so the correction is on the record. A limit the writer states is a limit the reader did not have to discover, and discovering one costs more trust than being told it. The tempting reading prefers the sentence that promises importance, and a claim about being the most important point makes no claim at all about the evidence, so it adds weight without adding anything a reader could weigh.
questions.hint: Ask which sentences hand the reader a limit on the piece's own claim.
questions.learningObjective: identify the sentences in which a piece concedes and thereby gains trust

options.text: This is the most important point in the whole argument

options.misconception: treats an impossibility claim as though it conceded a limit
options.text: Nobody could reasonably have predicted how this would turn out

questions.explanation: The second person turns a reported procedure into a scene the reader occupies, so the stakes arrive as anticipation rather than as information, and the writer gets the sequence of small physical details for free. That is what 'picture yourself' buys. The tempting reading hears an intrusion, since a writer has no business narrating a reader's feelings, but intrusion would be a claim about what the reader must have felt; this sentence supplies a place to stand and leaves the feeling unsaid, which is the difference between writing a reader into a scene and writing a reader's mind for them.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader now knows that the third person would not have told them.

options.text: It presumes the reader is frightened, which the piece never states

options.misconception: confuses vividness with a general account of how anyone feels
options.text: It replaces one particular account with a general one that fits anyone

questions.explanation: The register is the one a resource plan keeps, and it holds the reader at the distance from which a closure is an entry in a table. That distance is the problem: the news is about a service no longer within reach, and the register suppresses exactly the response the news is likely to produce. The tempting reading approves of the impersonal tone as the mark of an official notice, but an official notice reporting a decision is not the same as an official notice announcing one, and only the second has an audience whose response is at stake.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader is prevented from feeling by the register used.
questions.learningObjective: analyse what an impersonal register does to a reader's response to bad news

options.misconception: assumes the register was borrowed from a document being quoted
